item.title: The race for the most powerful AI model is nearing its end. Financial Times explains why businesses no longer need it
item.description:
For the past few years, tracking the development of generative AI has been like following a sports league table. OpenAI released GPT-4, Google responded with Gemini, Anthropic showcased its new Claude, and then the next round began. Each company presented a set of benchmarks and explained where its model was now leading. In 2026, this logic started to break down. Not because models stopped getting more powerful. On the contrary, on September 1st, Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.1, a new top-tier model for programming and complex intellectual work. The problem is different: the ability to build a stronger model no longer means that most clients will want to use it for most tasks. The Financial Times recently highlighted an illustrative example. Fable 5 was released on June 9, 2026, as one of Anthropic's most powerful models, but about two months later, it accounted for about 11% of Anthropic product spending among corporate clients tracked by Ramp. It's important to clarify here. This is not 11% of Anthropic's total revenue, but an indicator within a specific sample of corporate spending. Furthermore, Fable's initial launch was interrupted: on June 12, access to the model was disabled due to US export restrictions, and the global release was restored on July 1. Therefore, this figure cannot be used as a perfect measure of demand. But the trend itself is much more interesting than the specific 11%. Companies are increasingly choosing cheaper models if the additional quality of a frontier model does not affect the business outcome. Read more

item.title: Comparing Opus 5, Sol 5.6, Gemini Flash 3.7, 3.8, and Pro 3.1 in Literary Translation and Editing
item.description:

item.title: The AI Labor Revolution: From Machine-Centric to Human-Centric Division of Labor
item.description:
The modern concept of work, rooted in the Industrial Revolution, shifted the role of creator from human to machine, redefining the worker from a master of their craft to an operator of machine labor. Machines now perform most tasks, yet humans remain bound as appendages, forced to work at machine pace and within machine constraints. This is the antithesis of free, motivated, and meaningful work that truly defines humanity. The industrial concept of the 'worker' is dehumanizing; one is either human or a worker. The solution isn't regression, but completing the industrial revolution through automation, with AI serving as the thinking appendage to mechanisms. This is precisely why AI was invented.

item.title: LLM Loops: How to Find the Cause Without Touching Parameters?
item.description:
LLMs in production can appear stable for weeks, then start looping on a single paragraph, hitting token limits, and straining infrastructure without a single error in the logs. This article explores how to diagnose such failures: what signals help find the cause, why changing generation parameters is often the wrong first step, and how to build system-level defenses against repeated loops. Let's break down a case.

item.title: AI Everywhere Except in Performance Reports. What's Happening with the Economy and How Virtual Employees Will Save It
item.description:
If the news is anything to go by, we're on the cusp of a bright cybernetic future. Leading researchers claim that by 2026, up to 80% of large companies will be using generative AI. Nvidia's market capitalization is hitting historic highs, and venture capital funds are pouring money into AI startups. However, if you look at the macroeconomic reports from the US Federal Reserve or OECD Data, the picture is different. Global labor productivity is stagnating, growing by only 1-1.5% per year. There's no surge or technological breakthrough on a national scale reflected in real GDP figures. This creates a paradox: on one hand, there are colossal investments and reports of models surpassing humans, and on the other, statistics showing that the macroeconomy is oblivious to this boom. Who should we believe? Marketers hyping another bubble, or government agencies that haven't yet learned to evaluate new metrics? Economic forecasts are slowly shifting from assumptions like 'AI will replace half of all jobs' towards cautious econometric analysis. A balanced perspective can be found at the US National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER), which has formulated the idea that the economy is facing a phenomenon it already experienced forty years ago. In this article, we will examine recent scientific publications discussing the weaknesses that are hindering the bright AI future. Read more
